title: Longest Strictly Rising Stretch
statement:
You get an array nums, for example daily step counts. A rising stretch is a run of neighbouring positions where every value is strictly larger than the one before it.

Return the length of the longest rising stretch. A single value on its own is a stretch of length 1.

examples.why: [2, 3, 5, 7] has four values, each bigger than the last. [4, 6, 9] has only three.
5 → 5 is not a strict rise, so the run breaks there: [3, 5] and [5, 8] each have length 2.
Values must sit next to each other. 1, 2, 3, 4 is rising but skips the 9, so it does not count; [2, 3, 4] does.

hints: Walk the array once. What do you need to remember about the stretch that ends at the current position?
Only its length. If the current value beats the previous one, the stretch grows by one; otherwise a new one starts here.
Keep a running length that resets to 1 on any non-rise, and a best-so-far that you update after every step.

explain.intuition:
A rising stretch can only be broken in one way: a value that is not bigger than the one before it. So as you scan left to right, the stretch ending at position i is either the previous stretch plus one (if nums[i] > nums[i − 1]) or a fresh stretch of length 1.

That makes it a sliding window whose left edge only ever jumps forward to the break point. You never need to look back, so one pass with two numbers is enough. It is the same shape as tracking a "current streak" of daily logins.
steps: For every i from 1: if nums[i] > nums[i − 1], add one to run; otherwise set run = 1.
pitfalls: Using ≥ instead of >. Equal neighbours break the stretch.
Only updating best when the run breaks. If the longest stretch reaches the end of the array, it is never recorded.
Solving the subsequence version (values may skip positions). That is a different, harder problem.

solutions.title: Extend from every start
solutions.idea: From each position, walk right while the values keep rising, and keep the longest walk.

solutions.title: One pass with a running length
solutions.idea: The stretch ending here is the previous one plus one, or a fresh start of 1.

followups: Return the start and end index of the longest stretch, picking the leftmost on ties.
Allow one value to be changed. How long can the stretch get now?
